paras: The threatened lynching of William Neal took place in Wilmington, Delaware, on the afternoon of 6 December 1881, when a jury acquitted Neal, a Black man, of an alleged rape of a white woman, Mrs. Gosser. Because of threats to lynch him, he was hurried from the courtroom to a waiting carriage and driven out of the state into Pennsylvania. The case drew attention because the verdict was condemned across the state, and several papers warned that it would bring on lynch law in Delaware.

Neal, of Smyrna, was first tried at the May 1880 term, after his counsel, Mr. Higgins, failed in a motion to quash the jury panels for excluding men of African descent. That jury convicted him on 26 May 1880 and he was sentenced to hang, but the judgment was reversed and he was tried again in early December 1881. At the second trial the jury deliberated from Saturday evening to Tuesday afternoon and took twenty-one ballots, reportedly finding Mrs. Gosser's evidence contradictory in some points.

About three o'clock on Tuesday the foreman announced 'not guilty,' and the Chief Justice discharged Neal from custody. According to the Daily Republican, Neal was taken out between two tipstaves to a carriage that was 'in some mysterious manner' already waiting, and was driven off because of 'serious threats of lynching him,' both from people outside and from many in the courtroom. The Daily Gazette said he was placed in a close carriage later in the afternoon, for fear the public would not accept his acquittal, and was left at the State line above Claymont, in Delaware County, Pennsylvania.

On 8 December the Republican reported that Ex-Sheriff Herbert had said the next such case would not 'bother a jury' and that William Dean had said the jurors who cleared Neal should be hung. The same day Henry C. Mahaffy, Levy Court Commissioner from Brandywine Hundred, denied a report in a 'sensational paper' that Neal had stopped for supper at his house on the way to Pennsylvania. No attack on Neal and no arrest for the threats appear in the coverage.

The threats and Neal's removal were reported only by the two Wilmington dailies, which took opposite sides on the verdict. The Republican printed the headline 'Some Talk of Lynching the Released Man' and later mocked Herbert and Dean as 'law abiding citizens' whose remarks amounted to 'threats of lynching.' Although it also said it disagreed with the verdict, the Republican pointed out that for years only Black defendants had been executed while white ones were cleared, according to the Gazette's quotation of it.

The Gazette, under the headline 'Neal Escapes the Halter,' called Neal 'the black villain,' accused the defense of packing the jury with Republicans, and said the last holdout for conviction had joined 'the negro worshipers.' It did not mention the lynching threats but reported that Neal was 'spirited away to the North.' In the following days it reprinted editorials from the Smyrna Times and other Peninsula papers warning that the verdict would drive people to 'Judge Lynch,' one saying it had 'clothed Lynch Law with justice and respectability.'

The two dailies gave different reasons for Neal's hasty removal: the Republican cited lynching threats, while the Gazette spoke only of fear that the public would not accept his innocence. The 'sensational paper' story of a supper stop at Mahaffy's house is known only from his denial in the Republican.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Neal
bases: A Black man acquitted of an alleged rape was rushed from the courtroom in a carriage because of threats to lynch him (A3), and driven out of the state (A2); no attack on him is reported.

No one was killed or attacked; the papers report only threats of lynching from unnamed persons in and outside the courtroom (A3) and angry remarks by two named men (A4), prompted by the acquittal on a rape charge (A1, A3).

Both Wilmington dailies report that Neal was hurried off in a carriage after the verdict (A2, A3); only the Republican attributes this to 'threats of lynching' (A3, A5), while the Gazette says it was for fear the public would not accept his innocence (A2).

accounts.gist: Neal was hurried to a carriage provided 'in some mysterious manner' because of serious threats of lynching from people outside and inside the courtroom; the paper later named Herbert and Dean as the source of such threats.

accounts.label: Daily Gazette
accounts.gist: Neal was put in a close carriage later in the afternoon, for fear the public would not accept his innocence, and left at the State line above Claymont.

accounts.label: Unnamed 'sensational paper' (as reported by the Republican)
accounts.gist: Neal was taken in a closed carriage to Mahaffy's residence and given supper before crossing into Pennsylvania; Mahaffy called this a lie.

framing.detail: The Republican's headline 'Some Talk of Lynching the Released Man' reported the threats; it asked whether Herbert and Dean were 'law abiding citizens' and mocked them as such.

The Gazette ('Neal Escapes the Halter') called Neal 'the black villain', the jurors 'negro worshipers', and reprinted editorials saying the verdict 'clothed Lynch Law with justice and respectability'.
